section_summary: This section follows disputes over how to test, price and sell Japanese silk, alongside plans to revive silk production and organise SCAP’s textile administration. It then documents American cotton textile production, proposed export allocations, and Siam’s efforts to obtain textiles for its rice trade. The final, lengthy teleconference addresses textile prices, payments, allocations and production forecasts, with several other export questions.

subfiles.title: Silk export and tariff recommendations
subfiles.about: Magagna urges tariff clarification, broader silk sampling and an end to testing and sales bottlenecks.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum argues that silk exports could earn dollars needed for Japanese food imports. It recommends consulting U.S. customs authorities, sampling more grades of raw silk, considering barter for unsalable fabrics and reducing USCC’s control over exports.

subfiles.title: Proposed cable on U.S. retesting of raw silk
subfiles.about: SCAP challenges reliance on U.S. Testing Company and urges direct consultation with silk trade associations.
subfiles.summary: Claims commercial retesting delays sales and reduces returns.

subfiles.title: Draft cable on Japanese raw silk testing
subfiles.about: SCAP proposes using Japanese government tests and open auctions to speed raw silk sales.
subfiles.summary: The draft describes rising testing capacity at Kobe and Yokohama and proposes selling silk against Japanese certificates. It criticises U.S. retesting, sealed bids and consultation with a testing firm in place of industry groups.

subfiles.title: Payment for Export Commodities in Kind
subfiles.to: Chief, Economic and Scientific Section, GHQ, SCAP
subfiles.about: Magagna proposes paying Japanese silk producers partly with food and equipment.
subfiles.summary: Magagna warns that inadequate payment is damaging silk production and the occupation’s dollar earnings. He proposes barter using stored food and agricultural equipment, arguing that equitable returns would encourage producers to bring silk and other goods to market.

subfiles.title: Draft cable on duties on textile cloth
subfiles.about: SCAP requests urgent clarification of U.S. duties on silk and other cloth.
subfiles.summary: Offers to send personnel to settle the tariff question.

subfiles.title: Administrative Order No. 10: Textile Division
subfiles.about: The order creates a Textile Division and sets out its responsibilities.
subfiles.summary: Assigns oversight of textile production, controls, distribution and export advice.

subfiles.title: Draft request for silk samples to trade groups
subfiles.about: SCAP asks that samples of available Japanese silk be sent to prospective U.S. users.
subfiles.summary: Names New York textile groups and highlights 42 denier silk.

subfiles.title: Draft request for silk sampling abroad
subfiles.about: The silk adviser urges sampling Latin American and European markets.
subfiles.summary: Emphasises potentially large stocks of 42 denier silk.

subfiles.title: Fragment on Japanese silk testing certificates
subfiles.about: A draft argues for Japanese testing certificates and direct contact with silk trade associations.
subfiles.summary: Criticises U.S. retesting as costly and slow.

subfiles.title: Magagna telegram to Congressman Flood
subfiles.about: Magagna asks Flood to intervene in silk sales and sampling policy.
subfiles.summary: Opposes sealed bids and urges immediate sampling of 42 denier silk.

subfiles.title: Raw Silk Testing
subfiles.about: SCAP details Japanese testing capacity and proposes sales using Japanese certificates.
subfiles.summary: The Kobe and Yokohama testing houses are expected to expand capacity. SCAP argues that certificates sent by airmail could support New York sales and remove the delay of universal U.S. retesting; it also raises an offer to sell at open auction.

subfiles.title: Subject and security reference sheet
subfiles.about: A file sheet records the 894.655 subject reference.
subfiles.summary: Subject reference and security fields.

subfiles.title: Letter to Mr. Noonan
subfiles.about: The State Department replies to an inquiry about Japanese textile information.
subfiles.summary: The surviving OCR preserves the salutation and signature; Noonan’s later letter says this reply offered a Textile Mission report.

subfiles.title: Routing sheet for letter to Congressman Flood
subfiles.about: A routing sheet records the file reference for a reply to Congressman Flood.
subfiles.summary: File numbers and routing marks.

subfiles.title: Letter to Congressman Flood, closing page
subfiles.about: A reply to Flood was cleared with USCC and War Department officers.
subfiles.summary: Only its closing and clearance note are legible.

subfiles.title: Reply to USCC on textile export policy
subfiles.about: Whitman answers concerns from the Textile Export Association about Japanese textile exports.
subfiles.summary: The reply addresses textile machinery and export price adjustments.

subfiles.title: USCC forwards Textile Export Association letter
subfiles.about: USCC forwards an association letter to Richard May and seeks State Department comments.
subfiles.summary: Encloses the association’s letter.

subfiles.title: Questions on Japanese cotton textile exports
subfiles.about: The Textile Export Association requests answers about markets, prices, machinery and Japan’s future cotton programme.
subfiles.summary: Plams asks where Japanese goods made from American cotton will be sold and how prices will reflect higher costs. He seeks information on 1947 supply, Japanese textile capacity, machinery copying and reparations.

subfiles.title: Bangkok telegram on Siamese textile mission
subfiles.about: A Siamese mission would inspect Japanese textiles and seek authority after receiving concrete proposals.
subfiles.summary: Describes the mission’s preliminary mandate.

subfiles.title: Inquiry to Bangkok about textile procurement
subfiles.about: State asks whether Siam is dealing directly with SCAP and whether its mission has been accepted.
subfiles.summary: Requests clarification of contact and entry permission.

subfiles.title: Japanese Raw Silk Production
subfiles.about: Donovan forwards a press article on Japanese silk and cotton production.
subfiles.summary: The despatch reports a raw silk production drive, anticipated testing expansion, and coal and equipment shortages. It also notes new looms, releases of hoarded textiles and promised financing for mills.

subfiles.title: Helping Japan's Silk Production
subfiles.about: The article reports silk production measures and related textile industry developments.
subfiles.summary: Covers funding, power conversion, testing capacity, cotton looms and mill loans.

subfiles.title: Referral of textile report request
subfiles.about: The War Department refers a request for a report on Japan’s textile industry.
subfiles.summary: Forwards William Ryle & Co.’s letter.

subfiles.title: Request to War Department for textile report
subfiles.about: William Ryle & Co. requests the June 1946 Japanese textile industry report.
subfiles.summary: Seeks a copy for use in textile trade.

subfiles.title: Request to State Department for textile report
subfiles.about: William Ryle & Co. asks State for its June 1946 Japanese textile report.
subfiles.summary: Requests a copy to assist the firm’s trade.

subfiles.title: Reply to Ernest Halley
subfiles.about: State replies to Halley’s request for Japanese textile information.
subfiles.summary: Identifies the available report and lists enclosures.

subfiles.title: Japanese Cotton and Rayon Production
subfiles.about: The consul forwards a press article on June cotton and rayon output.
subfiles.summary: Reports modest cotton yarn growth, limited use of new American cotton and rising rayon production. The despatch summarises mill activity and the prospect of a larger July output.

subfiles.title: Cotton Yarn Output Increases
subfiles.about: The article gives June 1946 Japanese cotton and rayon production figures.
subfiles.summary: It reports cotton yarn and cloth output, stocks, spinning capacity and shortages of coal and supplies. A rayon section covers pulp, yarn, staple and cloth production, with comparative May and June figures.

subfiles.title: Japanese Silk Production
subfiles.about: The consul forwards an article reporting a June decline in Japanese raw silk output.
subfiles.summary: Coal and seasonal labour shortages reduced June production below May’s level and the official goal. The report also describes abandonment of a cocoon export plan and expected cocoon shortages.

subfiles.title: Japanese Raw Silk Industry
subfiles.about: The article describes a slight June fall in Japanese silk production.
subfiles.summary: Includes silk industry figures and cocoon supply concerns.

subfiles.title: Reply to John Noonan about missing report
subfiles.about: Whitman promises a replacement copy of the Textile Mission report.
subfiles.summary: Explains that demand has delayed the printed edition.

subfiles.title: Noonan requests missing Textile Mission report
subfiles.about: Noonan says the promised Textile Mission report has not arrived.
subfiles.summary: Asks Martin to check whether it was sent.

subfiles.title: Lustre Fibres requests Textile Mission report
subfiles.about: Mills requests a copy of the Textile Mission report on Rose’s suggestion.
subfiles.summary: Asks Whitman to send the newly issued report.

subfiles.title: Reply to George Mills
subfiles.about: Whitman answers Mills’s request for the Textile Mission report.
subfiles.summary: Cites heavy demand and promises a copy.

subfiles.title: Reply to Herbert Rose on Japanese cotton exports
subfiles.about: State acknowledges Rose’s recommendations for third-quarter Japanese cotton textile exports.
subfiles.summary: Says recommendations were sent to the War Department and USCC.

subfiles.title: Consultation with SCAP regarding the textile ration for Japan
subfiles.about: Whitman proposes conveying Far Eastern Commission views on Japan’s textile ration to SCAP.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum anticipates agreement on a simplified policy statement but continued pressure for a maximum ration. Whitman seeks authority to communicate commission views through its chairman, while leaving final determination of Japan’s needs to SCAP.

subfiles.title: Combined Textile Committee transmittal
subfiles.about: Rose submits the committee’s revised allocation recommendation for Japanese cotton textiles.
subfiles.summary: Requests review and action on allocations covering fabric, yarn and singlets.

subfiles.title: Combined Textile Committee Recommendation No. 9
subfiles.about: The committee approves and forwards its revised third-quarter allocation report.
subfiles.summary: Recommends implementation of Staff Report No. 4.

subfiles.title: Allocation of Japanese Cotton Textiles, Third Quarter 1946
subfiles.about: The report recommends destinations for 193 million yards of fabric, 8 million pounds of yarn and singlets.
subfiles.summary: The staff proposes retaining the distribution pattern of an earlier 120 million yard recommendation, reserving some cloth and singlets for special food-related programmes. A table allocates quantities among the Netherlands East Indies, Siam, Burma, British Far Eastern colonies, Indochina and the Philippines.

subfiles.title: Cotton Textiles Produced in Japan from U.S. Cotton Available for Export
subfiles.about: SCAP reports delayed cotton manufacturing and forecasts third-quarter export production.
subfiles.summary: The edited cable says cotton arrivals have fallen behind schedule but forecasts at least 110 million yards of cloth for third-quarter export. It lists proposed cloth types, 8 million pounds of sale yarn and about 800,000 pounds of singlets.

subfiles.title: Report on Japanese Cotton Textile Stocks
subfiles.about: SCAP describes available textile stocks, specifications and possible shipment dates.
subfiles.summary: The report inventories government, mill, military and dispersed piece-goods stocks, together with cloth produced from Japanese materials. It estimates 50 million yards for August delivery and a possible further 33 million for September, subject to specifications and allocation.

subfiles.title: Bangkok telegram on Siamese mission entry
subfiles.about: Bangkok reports that SCAP has not authorised a Siamese textile mission to enter Japan.
subfiles.summary: Says Siam communicates through the U.S. Legation.

subfiles.title: Letter to H. Wickliffe Rose
subfiles.about: Whitman acknowledges Rose’s help circulating the Textile Mission report.
subfiles.summary: Notes heavy demand and promises a copy.

subfiles.title: Request for Entry of Siamese Textile Purchasing Mission into Japan
subfiles.about: Whitman urges SCAP to admit a Siamese purchasing mission to expedite textile shipments.
subfiles.summary: Links Siam’s 30 million yard allocation to rice procurement.

subfiles.title: Urgent instruction to secure Siamese mission entry
subfiles.about: State asks SCAP to admit Siam’s textile mission and expedite textile procurement.
subfiles.summary: The telegram recounts repeated unanswered requests and Siam’s 30 million yard allocation. It says textiles are needed as consumer incentives for rice growers and merchants and asks SCAP to clarify the position, grant entry and help deliveries.

subfiles.title: Bangkok urgent request for mission entry
subfiles.about: Bangkok asks State to obtain SCAP permission for Siam’s textile mission.
subfiles.summary: Reports that SCAP replies called the sender unidentifiable.

subfiles.title: Bangkok clarification of textile negotiations
subfiles.about: Bangkok clarifies Siam’s shipping and negotiation position and again urges mission entry.
subfiles.summary: Siam sought SCAP shipping help and authorised only preliminary discussions, including possible barter, pending concrete proposals.

subfiles.title: Washington–Tokyo teleconference on textile exports and other commodities
subfiles.from: Washington conferees led by Arthur Gardiner
subfiles.to: Tokyo conferees led by A. L. Barber
subfiles.about: Officials discuss Japanese cotton textile prices, allocations, payments, production and several other export issues.
subfiles.summary: Washington and Tokyo agree to use U.S. export ceiling prices, arrange detailed fabric allocations in Tokyo and handle contracts in Washington; they debate whether British and Siamese buyers must pay dollars. Tokyo reports capacity, yarn output and prospective fourth-quarter fabric exports, while the parties discuss delays caused by labour, food, coal and power shortages. Further exchanges cover silk insurance and habutae, finishing chemicals, cotton blankets, other commodities, fertilizer, aluminium, soda ash and handicraft samples.
